native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Using World Bank group-level data (1975-2015), education expenditure is measured as adjusted savings for education as a share of GNI (NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS) and income as GNI per capita in constant 2015 US$ (NY.GNP.PCAP.KD). For lower-middle-income (developing) countries, the association between changes in the education-expenditure share and per-capita GDP growth is small and contemporaneous - a 1 percentage-point higher share in a given year is associated with roughly 4 percentage points higher growth in that same year (beta = 0.040, t = 2.6, n = 40) and becomes insignificant at 1- and 5-year lags, while the level association is actually negative (beta ~ -0.2) once the common time trend is controlled. For Sub-Saharan Africa, per-capita income is observed only for 2011-2015, a window in which the education-expenditure share fell from 3.65% to 3.15% of GNI while GNI per capita rose from US$1,555 to US$1,634 - a negative co-movement (r = -0.97, n = 5, descriptive only). The data therefore do not support the hypothesis that education expenditure is associated with per-capita GDP more strongly in Sub-Saharan Africa than among developing (lower-middle-income) countries; if anything, the data suggest the association is weak in both groups and cannot be reliably estimated for Sub-Saharan Africa from this five-year window.
native_result.WorkflowB: Pivoted the 12-row wide CSV to group x series panels. LMC: OLS level model ln(GNIpc_t) ~ edu_{t-k} + linear trend and growth model dln(GNIpc_t) ~ d(du_{t-k}) + linear trend for k in {0,1,5}, reporting beta, SE, t, p, R2, n. SSA: 5-point (2011-2015) descriptive statistics (means, ranges, directions) and Pearson correlations explicitly labeled non-inferential. Structured comparison of the two groups' associations and a data-grounded hypothesis drafted with non-causal language.
